utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Registrar, have the accused brought in, please. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume the hearing. First I would like to ask whether the interpreters are ready. Yes. I would like to wish everybody a happy new year, all people who are working with us in this trial. First of all, does everybody hear? Does the Prosecutor hear, the Defence hear? Does the accused hear? General Blaskic, do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLASKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honour, I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can then start again. Let me first turn to the Prosecutor and ask him, what is on this week's programme? I understood there were a lot of witnesses. Perhaps the order which we made about the testimony of witnesses, we can hope that this will speed things up a bit. Mr. Prosecutor, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President and your Honours. Happy new year to you as well and to counsel. Mr. President, we have a number of witnesses this week, as you can see we have, and we will proceed with them in as quick an order as we can. The first witness I will be calling this afternoon, Mr. President, is Munib Kajmovic. I can start with identifying those parts of the indictment about which Mr. Kajmovic's testimony is relevant. First, Mr. President, his testimony is relevant to paragraph 5.2 of the general allegations section of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And is relevant to count 1, persecution, crimes against humanity, dealing with the forcible transfer of civilians, paragraphs 6.6, 6.7 and paragraph 7. To summarise Mr. Kajmovic's testimony, Mr. Kajmovic is from Central Bosnia, he was born in the Travnik Municipality and he lived in Vitez from 1976 until 1994, the last eleven months of which he was in Stari Vitez, involved in the siege of Stari Vitez as a defender. From 1976 until April 1993, he was a history teacher at the Vitez High School. While he was a resident of Vitez, he was active in civil and political affairs, including being the President of the SDA, the Bosnian Muslim political party in Vitez. In 1994, following the end of the siege of Stari Vitez, Mr. Kajmovic enrolled for graduate studies at the University of Sarajevo, School of Politics, where as part of his studies for a Master's degree he prepared a Master's thesis entitled "Political and Demographic Changes in the Vitez Municipality between 1992 and 1995". His thesis will be presented this June in front of the Faculty of the University of Sarajevo and we will offer him as an expert in the area of demographic changes in the Vitez Municipality during the time-frame which I have just identified. His testimony will be limited to testifying about the results of his research into the demographic changes in the Vitez Municipality as a result of the war. He will describe the manner and methods he used in preparing his report and he will present evidence of his findings and conclusions in respect of the demographic changes of ethnic population movement in the Vitez Municipality between 1991 and 1995 and the causes for those changes. So that, Mr. President, is a summary of what he will testify about before this Trial Chamber today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Speaking about an expert, and with the concerns we have in trying to make sure everything is done as quickly as possible, whether there is a cross-examination in any case, did this expert submit a report which would allow everybody to see it and to be sure that only the most important questions are asked?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, we did not submit a report to the Defence. As part of the court's order, a copy of which I have, the Prosecutor was not required -- the parties are not required to submit expert reports. That was part of the decision of this chamber, and I can refer the Trial Chamber to that part of the decision if the court so please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Under those conditions, we have heard your answer, you can have the witness, Mr. Kajmovic, brought in. I believe that is the name. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me, Mr. Kajmovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please turn to me, direct your answers to me, please. Tell us your name, surname and first name. Please look at the President when you are answering. That is right, because I am the one speaking to you. Tell me your name and first name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Munib Kajmovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. While remaining standing you are going to read the declaration which the usher is going to give to you. MR. MUNIB KAJMOVIC (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated, Mr. Kajmovic. You were called by the Prosecutor as part of the trial of the accused who is here, General Blaskic. The Prosecutor has summarised what you are going to tell us and after a few initial questions you will speak freely and then answer any questions which the Prosecutor will ask you. Mr. Prosecutor, I give you the floor, if you wish to begin now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Mr. Kajmovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am going to ask you some preliminary questions and then we will turn directly to the heart of your testimony. Mr. Kajmovic, are you 51 years old?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina and a Muslim by faith?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you born in the Travnik Municipality in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You could perhaps move a little closer, it might make it a little easier for you to testify. That is fine. Mr. Kajmovic, did you earn a Bachelor of Arts degree in history from the University of Sarajevo in 1974?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thereafter, did you become a teacher of history at the Vitez High School from 1976 until April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While you were living in the Vitez Municipality, were you active in the civil and political affairs of that community, including being the President of the Muslim political party, the SDA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you remain in Vitez Municipality until 1994, that is after the end of the siege of Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now let me turn your attention to the area that I have asked you to come here to testify about, and that is a study that you undertook regarding demographics. First of all, Mr. Kajmovic, can you tell the judges about when you enrolled at the University of Sarajevo, the degree that you are pursuing, the topic of your Master's thesis in general terms, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. From earlier on, I had a wish to pursue scholarship on a more serious level, but that was not possible at that time. After the armed conflict between the HVO and the BiH army, I decided to enrol into the graduate studies at the University of Sarajevo School of Political Science. This was in late 1994, and after about a year and a half, after I passed the exams required by the curriculum, by the programme of the graduate studies, I applied to the Lectures Council at the school to approve my thesis, whose topic was "The Demographic Changes in the Municipality of Vitez between 1992 and 1995". The faculty considered my application and they approved it eventually. I was assigned a professor who was going to be the mentor, who was going to follow the project and who was going to -- with whom I was going to consult. The faculty decided that this person should be the doctor Mirko Pejanovic, who is the professor in the -- Mr. Pejanovic was also a member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina at one point. After this topic was approved, I started my work on this project, and I am almost at the end of it. I should, this next June, I am supposed to defend this paper at the School of Political Science. The topic is also of certain interest to the Tribunal, as I understand, and since I have given a statement regarding the events in Vitez, and so it happened that these -- there has been a confluence of interests here, and I can speak to certain results that I have reached researching this topic as regards the Municipality of Vitez. I do not know whether I should move on and start to elaborate on the topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me just ask you, you mentioned Dr. Mirko Pejanovic. He is a Serb, is he not? A Bosnian Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he is an ethnic Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Before getting into your actual research, can you tell the court a little bit about the Vitez municipality itself, its size, its dimensions, certain characteristics about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the Vitez Municipality is one of the smaller municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Its square area is 159 square kilometres, and it has 28,000 inhabitants. The municipality is populated in its northern part. Ethnically the population was mixed, approximately 45 per cent of the population were Bosnian Croats, about 41 per cent Bosniaks, about 5 per cent Bosnian Serbs. 4 point something per cent were Yugoslavs and the rest were others. Until --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, before we get into your actual data, could you inform the court how you went about collecting the data for your thesis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When working on this thesis, of course I had to use certain sources, and since this is the issue of demographic changes that we are dealing with here, as a basis I used the census of 1991; that was the starting point. After that, I used sources that were institutions of legal powers of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the territory of the Vitez Municipality; I used data of the Territorial Defence headquarters, and then there was an internal census that was taken at the end of 1995 in the territory of the municipality that was under the control of the BiH army. I also used data of the service of the local commune of Vitez, that was the Bosniak part. Then I used Red Cross Vitez data. I also used the data of the Merhamet Society, except for those data I also relied heavily on my own research in the field. Given that the Vitez Municipality is fairly small in size, that the area of the territory of the municipality is relatively small and that I knew quite a few people very well, I was able to do some personal research and I got some relevant data on that basis. So from that point of view, I had no problem in getting to the sources and to provide an objective picture of the demographics. What I had problems with was the part of the territory that was under the control of the HVO, because the relations there are still such that there is absolutely no possibility -- there is not even a possibility of free movement, let alone getting hold of certain data, so there I had to apply different methods. There I had to start with a data basis which was based on the census that was done in 1991, and then I did some indirect research in the field. I did that in several local communes, that is those administrative units. There were five or six such administrative territorial units where I indirectly gathered data. The way I gathered this data was basically this. In these local communes, Bosnian Croats had not moved, so the data from 1991 was unchanged. So from those territories, the Bosnians had moved, and other ethnic groups, and I -- so I gathered this data in such a way that I used the 1991 data, that is the average members per household was 3.70 persons. Then I applied this number to other data that I received from the field: that is, Bosniaks would visit these local communes, they would go to their cemeteries, and they gathered data how many Bosniak houses were burnt down or destroyed; in other words that were uninhabited. I already had the data on a number of such households, so I used that data that they gave me on the functional households and whether they are inhabited. Then on the basis of this information, I multiplied the number of these households by 3.7, and I got the data on the number of the Bosnian Croats who were resident there, so these data are not absolutely accurate, but everything points to maybe 5 to 6 points of error margin at the most. So this is how I arrived at the structure, the numbers of the Bosnian Croats in the Vitez Municipality. When I gathered all the relevant data, I could then proceed to analyse and to precisely determine what the demographic structure was in 1991, and what the situation was in 1995. My position is that the information is fairly accurate, especially when it regards the demographic changes in the area of the municipality which is under the control of the BiH army; that is the changes that reflect the changes among the Bosniaks. I also feel that the data regarding the Bosnian Croats are reliable, but still I have certain reservations there, because there could be an error margin of 5 to 6 points there. So basically, this is the technology and the method of work which I applied to this particular topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, in the course of collecting your data, one of the most important parts of your data collection included interviews with people in the community itself and displaced persons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. For all the local communes and inhabited settlements from which the Bosniaks were removed, I talked to the local residents and I gathered the data. It was not such a difficult task, because there were not that many people and then there were not many communes like that, so there were not large numbers. I know all these local communes well and a fair number of people too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, let us start then with your demographic data for 1991 for the Vitez municipality and in that regard, let me have the usher bring to you the first binder which contains three exhibits which, Mr. Dubuisson, I believe would be exhibits 192, 193 and 194; is that correct? Mr. President and your Honours, in respect of 192, there is a French and English translation attached. The same is true with 193 and there is neither an English nor a French translation for 194, because reproducing it in French and English would have lost the colours that are found on exhibit 194. It is not a very complex exhibit and I think we can read or have the witness read the script on 194 if the court please. Mr. Usher, if you could put those exhibits before the witness, the three exhibits. Mr. Kajmovic, what I would like you to do, if you would, would you kindly explain to the judges, using exhibits 192, 193 and 194 what your findings were in respect of the demographic data for 1991. I have informed you earlier on how to use the ELMO, so if you just place those items on the ELMO as you testify, we can then proceed, I think, in a very effective manner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shall I open this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You do not have to disassemble them. There should be a version on the top which is in your language that you can work from. It should come up in front of you on the video screen. If we could focus in on that complete exhibit, this is exhibit 192, Mr. President and counsel. If you could explain, Mr. Kajmovic, what that exhibit represents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Here we have the borders of the Municipality of Vitez. This is the dotted line . Then we have the administrative territorial division of the Municipality of Vitez into 17 local communes, which are marked with numbers from 1 to 17, and in the right-hand corner, we have the list of the names of those local communes, so this is the administrative territorial division of the Municipality of Vitez into these smaller units. That is what is shown on this exhibit. Here we also have the names of the neighbouring municipalities bordering on the Municipality of Vitez. North of Vitez is the Municipality of Zenica. Then to the north-west is the Municipality of Travnik. To the east is the Municipality of Busovaca, and to the northern part is the neighbouring Municipality of Novi Travnik, which is not shown on the screen, and a small segment of the Municipality of Fojnica, which also borders on the Municipality of Vitez. Now you can see it. Here it is, Novi Travnik (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Kajmovic, if you would then explain the demographic data for the Vitez Municipality in 1991 using the other exhibits in front of you. You can remove the exhibit in front of you and place other exhibits on the ELMO as you wish in making your explanation. Mr. Usher, I think Mr. Kajmovic will be able to manipulate those three exhibits for the time being. If he has difficulty, I will ask you to assist. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here on the screen we have a table of the ethnic composition of the population of the Vitez municipality according to the 1991 census. The composition of the population is worked out by inhabited places, and it is indicated how many people lived in each local community, according to the 1991 census, and also how that population was composed ethnically. So at the bottom line, it shows the sum, the total number of inhabitants. In the first column, we have the number of Bosnian Croats living there, according to the 1991 census, in each of the local communes and at the bottom, the sum total. In those same local communes, we have indicated in the second column the percentage share of the Croats. Then in the third column the figures are given for the number of Bosniaks living in the Municipality of Vitez, in the same local communes, and, by looking at those columns crosswise, we can see the ethnic composition, how many people of which ethnic origin inhabited which local commune. Then we can see the percentage share in the fourth column. The fifth column indicates the number of Serbs, then the sixth column their percentage share in the total. Then the number of Yugoslavs in the next column, their percentage share, and finally what was known as "Others", their percentage share, and at the end we have the total population of the Vitez Municipality according to the 1991 census, and the percentages. Therefore the table gives a review of the ethnic composition and, of course, the number of inhabitants of the Vitez Municipality, and it served as a basis for monitoring all other demographic changes that took place in the Municipality, and it was done on the basis of the statistical book of the Statistics Institute of Bosnia-Herzegovina. According to this table, in 1991, there were 12,675 Bosnian Croats living in the Vitez Municipality, or 45.49 per cent of the population. Then there were 11,514 Bosniaks or 41.2 per cent. Then there were 1,501 Bosnian Serbs, or 5.38 per cent; 1,377 Yugoslavs or 4.94 per cent, and 792 others, or 2.84 per cent, or the total population was 27,859.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, for the record, you have been referring to exhibit number 193. Now if you could turn to exhibit 194 and explain to the Trial Chamber what exhibit 194 is. First of all, place it on the ELMO. First of all we need to get a focus on that complete exhibit. Could you move it up a little, Mr. Kajmovic, so it appears fully in the screen? That is fine, thank you. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber what this exhibit represents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This exhibit indicates the ethnic composition of the population of the Vitez Municipality in 1991, but also how that population was distributed, so it is easy to see. In this document, here in the frame we have dots in various colours, blue dots indicating the number of Croats, Bosnian Croats in the Municipality of Vitez, since according to the census there were 45 per cent Bosnian Croats. On this document we have 45 dots, blue dots, so each dot stands for 1 per cent of the Bosnian Croats out of the total population of Vitez Municipality. Those blue dots are distributed on the table where they actually lived, so that we can see from those blue dots how the ethnic group, that is the Bosnian Croats, were distributed in the Vitez Municipality, and we can also see the ethnic mix of the population, that they were mixed together. The green dots on the document indicate the Bosniaks and their distribution within the Municipality. The red dots are the Bosnian Serbs and their distribution in the municipality, then the brown or black dots are the Yugoslavs, and finally we have the white circles or white dots, indicating the others, the so-called "Others", because we had some other ethnic groups, which come under the heading of "Others". So this is a visual presentation of the population mix. Then here we also have a graphic presentation of this circle, indicating the percentage share of each group in the population, as we have already shown in the previous table.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right, thank you. If the usher could now reassemble that particular exhibit, but leave it at the side of Mr. Kajmovic, we could now turn to a different set of exhibits, but let me begin by asking you a question, Mr. Kajmovic. During the war the Vitez Municipality was eventually divided into portions that were exclusively controlled by the HVO and other portions of the Vitez Municipality. They were exclusively controlled by the ABiH; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In respect of the next set of exhibits which will be 195 through 199, I would ask you to explain your findings in the area that was exclusively controlled by the HVO. Please discuss with the judges your findings in respect of the displacement of ethnic groups within that area and the causes for that displacement. If you can identify by number, if you can, Mr. Kajmovic, the number of the exhibit that you have placed on the ELMO so we can refer to it later in the record?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is exhibit 195.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you now explain to the court what exhibit 195 represents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document shows the Vitez Municipality. These are the boundaries of the municipality. Then it also shows the lines when a cessation of hostilities took place on 25th February 1995. Actually, those lines of confrontation, this is this line -- line of separation rather -- and in the southern part of the municipality, there is this line (indicates). Here we have a small section which is under the control of the BiH army in the centre. The green circles indicate the positions of the BiH army on 25th February 1994, and the blue triangles indicate the military positions of the HVO. Those would be the lines of separation of military forces on 25th February when the truce came into effect; that is the Washington Agreement came into force, but later, as can be seen, a final line of separation was drawn. The document shows which part of the Vitez Municipality remained in the control of the BiH army, and which part of the municipality remained in the control of the HVO, so this part, inside remained under the control of the HVO; and this part (indicates) under the control of the BiH army, as well as this part here, under the BiH army control, and this small segment here in the centre, called Stari Vitez, it is still under the control of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now Mr. Kajmovic, could you turn to your next exhibit which perhaps illustrates that even more clearly, which is exhibit 196. You have now put 196 on the ELMO, and that shows, does it not, Mr. Kajmovic, with the fleurs-de-lis the areas controlled by the ABiH and the chequer board indicates the area controlled by the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Here we have one line now, that is the final line , delineated in the negotiations between the representatives of the army and the HVO, so the space between the two lines does not exist any more. There is the final line of territorial separation, so this area is under the control of the HVO and the these two parts, plus this small segment here, under the control of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and these symbols indicate under whose control the area is, which part and how big a part. Let me also just add that the percentage share of the territory, of the area of 159 square kilometres, of that 75 per cent is under BiH army control and 25 per cent under HVO control and this can be seen here where the percentage is indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, now turning to the remaining exhibits in this particular package, could you explain to the court your findings in respect of the ethnic displacement of the various groups within the area, the zone controlled by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the previous documents, we were able to see that there was a mixture of ethnic groups in the territory of the municipality, and it was to a considerable degree in evidence in this area too, which is now under the control of the HVO. After the cessation of hostilities, an entirely different ethnic composition was created as compared to what we had in 1991. I was extremely intrigued by this problem; that is I wanted to see why this ethnic displacement had taken place, whether it was perhaps the military and political goal to achieve this ethnic separation of the population, and that was an additional motive for me to delve into these issues. Then I established what the changes were. The ethnic changes did not occur only in this area under the control of the HVO, of course. Certain ethnic displacements occurred also in this area that is under the control of the BiH army, but the reasons are quite different that led to this. The reasons are absolutely not the same, nor are the causes the same. The causes and reasons are quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, could you use the other exhibits that are part of this package to illustrate the demographic changes? What is the exhibit number on that, please, Mr. Kajmovic? If you turn it over, that should perhaps be exhibit 197; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is exhibit 197. Actually, here we have two tables, but I should like to turn back for a moment to exhibit 196, to show you which part of the territory we are referring to. That is the question that I wish to address. We are talking about changes in this part of the territory (indicates). So here we have two tables, showing what the population structure of the population was in this area that I showed a moment ago in 1991. It can be seen from this document that there were 11,704 Bosnian Croats living in that area, or 60.2 per cent; that there were 4,691 Bosniaks, or 24.12 per cent; that there were 1,240 Serbs or 6.3 per cent; 1,081 Yugoslavs, or 5.6 per cent; others 725 or 3.72 per cent, which makes a total of 19,441 inhabitants in this part of the territory, which was under the control of the HVO after the cessation of hostilities. The second table tells us how many people were expelled from that part of the territory, people of non-Croatian ethnicity. Therefore the second table shows that -- we have the number of 4,611 Bosniaks expelled from that area, who had lived there until 1991. Then the number of Serbs, 1,140, and it should be noted however that the Serbs were not expelled after all, they were not expelled. They did not leave the territory of Vitez Municipality under pressure. They mostly left prior to the outbreak of the conflict, that is before 16th April 1993, upon the call of SDS and Karadzic. Then we have the Yugoslavs, 437 and others, 470, which makes a total of 6,658 inhabitants who had lived there in 1991, are no longer living in this area which is under the control of the HVO, so that is the substance of this second table, and this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Kajmovic. Testify if you would in a narrative form, informing the court and counsel of your findings using all of the exhibits before you. This next exhibit, Mr. Kajmovic, I take it is 198; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, 198. We saw from the previous document that 6,658 persons or inhabitants were expelled from this area under the control of the HVO, with the exception that the Serbs were not expelled, that is 1,140 of them. . Among those expelled were 4,611 Bosniaks. I studied this problem in order to find out where they sought shelter, where they were expelled to and where they have continued to live after the cessation of hostilities and I established and showed on this table where they are currently residing. Within the Municipality of Vitez, 1,128 Bosniaks stayed behind, so they moved to that part of the municipality which was under the control of the BiH army. Then 2,779 Bosniaks found some sort of accommodation in the neighbouring municipality of Zenica, and they continued to live there. Then 516 Bosniaks found a new home in the 4 of Travnik; 113 went to other municipalities like Novi Travnik, Kakanj and so on and 75 of them left Bosnia-Herzegovina and went abroad. So this table tells us where those people moved to after being expelled. On this exhibit, we also have a graph of those displaced Bosniaks, so this first column tells us that 24.45 per cent of them remained within the territory of Vitez Municipality; the second group of 60.26 per cent in the territory of Zenica; 11.19 per cent went to the Travnik municipality, and 2.45 per cent to other municipalities, and 1.62 per cent abroad. Of course we do not have documents here to show what the situation is as regards Bosnian Croats, because with a few exceptions, they have remained within the territory of Vitez Municipality, or rather in the area under the control of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Kajmovic, with other exhibits that are attached in this set. Now I believe you are referring to exhibit 199; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, 199. This exhibit shows the ethnic composition of the population also in the part of the territory of Vitez Municipality which is under HVO control in 1995, so we are talking only about that part of the municipality, and this table gives us figures for that. From this table, we see by local communes, but perhaps it is more interesting to follow the bottom line of figures, because these are sum totals, showing the following facts. In this area, the first column, we have the figure of 15,221, that is a number indicating that at the end of 1995, there were 15,221 Bosnian Croats living in that area. This column shows -- if it is compared with the situation in 1991, then we see that there are more Croats there now, a little more than 2,500 more than there were in 1991. The second column says that it is 93.38 per cent. Then we see how many Bosniaks have remained in that area by local communes, and if we will look up the column from top to bottom, we will see a lot of zeros there, because there are no Bosniaks at all living there, and at the end you have the figure of 80, which means that out of the 4,611 Bosniaks, only 80 remain, and they are living in this area under the control of the HVO. The third column, or rather the fifth column, gives us the number of Serbs. There are about 100 of them and we know that in 1991 there were 1,501 of them, but in their case, as we have already pointed out, it was a political decision of the SDS and they moved out of the Vitez Municipality voluntarily. Then columns 6 and 7 indicate the number of Yugoslavs, 664, and finally others, 255, which tells us that in the area under HVO control at the end of 1995, there were 16,300 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, the bar chart that is underneath that table reflects the various percentages and totals of the various ethnic groups living in the HVO-controlled area in 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I think that is self-explanatory: it just reflects, does it not, Mr. Kajmovic, the figures and the percentages that are reflected in the table above it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In here we have a graph just reflecting the data from up above, so the first column shows that 15,221 Bosnian Croats were living in that area, and the rest of the bars just show the rest of them. The Bosniaks are 0.49 per cent, the Serbs 0.61, the Yugoslavs 3.95 and the others 1.58. So the demographic picture has been changed considerably in comparison to what was there in 1991, so between 1991 and 1995 there has been a considerable change and now it is basically a single ethnic group area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In respect of the displacement of the Muslim population in the HVO controlled territory, can you identify the causes of that displacement to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The Bosniak population for the most part has been expelled from the territory under the control of the HVO and it was expelled under pressure, so this was a policy whose goal and whose means was the so-called ethnic cleansing of the area; that is the expulsion of the population, Bosniaks most of all, and so that was both the goal and that was the means. There were different forms of pressure, so that this population would leave this area under the control of the HVO. What forms were these? It was breaking into apartments and houses, threat at gun point, abuse of -- various forms of abuse of people, and from the start of the hostilities, within three or four months they had to leave this area, so they were leaving under pressure and they were crossing the front-lines and moving into the area of the municipality under the control of the army. Some of the population also left the area controlled by the HVO in the form of exchanges, the population exchanges. That was a smaller percentage, but part of the population was also, so to speak, expelled in this way from the area controlled by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So Mr. Kajmovic, did your findings support the fact that after the cease-fire in April 1993, some number of Muslims remained in the HVO-controlled portions of the Vitez Municipality, but they were ultimately forced out by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned that 4,011 Bosniaks were expelled. Until the attack of the HVO, they lived in their own houses. After this attack, in the first few days, part of the population was expelled, and in cases like Ahmici, there was a genocide perpetrated, so there were some Bosnians who were expelled like in Gacice and Veceriska, local communes, so that was the part of municipalities that was the villages, and there for the most part people were already expelled in the first days of the conflict, and the rest of them, about 1,600 lived in the urban part of Vitez, in the town of Vitez. This part of the population had a different fate. They had no possibility of escape. They had no opportunity to reach the territory under the control of the BiH army, because they were surrounded by the HVO front lines, so they were at home, they could not move, and part of that population was arrested by the HVO and taken to the camps, like the SDK building, the People's University, the elementary school in Dubravica, the veterinary station. For the most part, the conscripts were arrested and detained. After three or four days, some kind of a cease-fire was established which again was not respected, and after this period a gradual expulsion of these 1,600 Bosniaks ensues from the urban part of Vitez. A smaller percentage, feeling threatened and unsafe, looked for ways to leave this urban area of Vitez that was under the control of the HVO. I established this through interviews. I found out that they were looking for different channels and contacts, even Croatian friends, so that they would find ways to cross the front-lines, but the majority of the population was expelled in such a way that the HVO soldiers would break into their homes. They would give them deadlines, sometimes they would be a couple of hours, sometimes one day, for them to leave their houses or apartments. There was a case for instance, Niroga Mulahalilovic had the experience that his former student appeared, he said, "You know, director, I feel very awkward but I am here to tell you that you have to leave your apartment", so he collected a few belongings and then he crossed the front-line. In any event, the methods were different, but behind them all, there was an element of force that was employed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now Mr. Kajmovic, I would like to turn to the next set of exhibits with the assistance of the usher. They will be exhibits 200 and 201, and these exhibits will focus your attention on those parts of the Vitez municipality that remained under the control of the ABiH. Can you please explain to the Trial Chamber and to counsel your findings in respect of the movement of ethnic populations from the areas controlled by the ABiH, and please use these exhibits that are before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document, number 200 -- we cannot see it now on the monitor. I do not know if I pushed anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I cannot see it either.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe I touched something here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We seem to have a technical problem, Mr. President. I do not know if you are getting an image on your screens, I am not on mine, and Mr. Kajmovic is not on his.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps we could continue anyway, because the judges have the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fine. Here is a document similar to the previous one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We do not have them, Mr. Dubuisson, do we? Let the witness explain the documents, even if we do not see them on the screens. We do not want to waste any time. Meanwhile the technicians will try to fix it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Does your Honour have a set of these documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, we do. When I said we do not have it, I meant we do not have it on our screens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a document similar to the previous one, except that it reflects the demographic changes in the territory of the Vitez Municipality under the control of the ABiH, so the first chart reflects the ethnic structure of the population in 1991 in the area under the control of the Army of BiH, and there we see that in 1991 there were 971 Bosnian Croats in the first horizontal column, 6,823 Bosniaks; 261 Serbs, 296 Yugoslavs, 67 others, a total of 8,418, and then this is also reflected in percentages. The second chart, we have figures on the population that has been moved from the territory under the control of the army, and here the data reflects that 946 Bosnian Croats were moved; the second column is empty, because there were no movements of Bosniaks; 254 Bosnian Serbs, 22 Yugoslavs and others 21; a total of 1,243. The second table shows that 946 Croats moved, and I need to explain this move.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, before you explain that move, the ELMO is now functional again, so if you could place that on the ELMO, your chart, the public will have the benefit of your testimony as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My research confirmed some of the political knowledge that we already had about the movements of the Bosniaks in the Vitez Municipality. It is similar to the other area in Central Bosnia. We have a particular principle here at work. In the areas that were not -- that did not come under the HVO control, so we are talking about the area that is not under the HVO control and there was movement of Croatian population, the reasons were the following. The HVO followed very strictly a principle which was that at any cost Bosnian Croats be moved to the areas that were under their military control, so from the areas where there was no HVO military control to the area where they had the military control, and they used all kinds of means. It was the propaganda, the Croats were invited to leave the areas under the control of the army and move to the areas under the control of the HVO. Speaking specifically of the Vitez municipality, there were two forms of movement of the Bosnian Croats from the area which came under the control of the BiH army. One part of Croats left the area which, as it later turned out, remained under the control of the BiH army. In the night between 15th and 16th April, so that night, part of the Bosnian Croats left the area which remained under the control of the BiH army. This example is the one we have in the Stari Vitez. There were a number of families who lived in the lower part, and during that night, they moved to the part of town that had been under the HVO control even prior to 16th April. About 20 Croats remained in Stari Vitez though. Then another part of Croats, about 400 from Poculica local commune, on the morning of the 16th which was when the conflict started, and since they could not control that area militarily, this number of about 400 Croats withdrew; that is they moved in those early morning hours to the part of town and the area that was under the control of the HVO; that is the area around Dubravica and farther towards Vitez. So for the most part, this move by the Bosnian Croats took place partly on the eve of the attack and the rest, the larger percentage, happened within a day or two after that. I also want to stress that the 400 Croats from Poculica withdrew when the armed conflict started between the army and the HVO. It is at that point that they moved out and withdrew to this area. I reached no conclusion as to any kind of pressure that these Croats had to move out; in fact for about a year I was Commander of the civilian defence there, and we always took efforts to make sure that these Croats also received the same humanitarian aid that the rest of the population did. It should not be discounted that a certain amount of pressure had been exercised on some of the Croats to move out of this area. I want to also stress that out of 946 Croats, most of them moved out in the first couple of days, so this movement of Croatian population for the most part happened at that time. But again I want to stress that there was no pressure except maybe for some individual cases which cannot be excluded in the events of that kind. So this is what this document speaks of. I believe that I have explained that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, yet another document in front of you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, right. Let me just add that a total of 1,243 persons moved out of the area under the control of the Army of BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, could you also turn to a table and a graph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I just want to verify one point. You said that most of those who moved moved in the first couple of days. What do you mean "the first couple of days"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think the first or first two days, meaning 16th and 17th April. The night of 15th /16th, the day of the 16th and the following day of 17th April 1993, so what I have in mind is 16th and 17th April 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, in front of you is exhibit 201. If we could get the proper focus on that exhibit it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, you are going to testify first of all about the table -- on the ELMO, if the focus could be brought down on the table itself, so the figures could be seen clearly. Mr. Kajmovic, perhaps if you could centre that diagram, or perhaps the usher can assist in this case. Mr. Usher, if you could show just the table, the top part of that diagram, centre it there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document reflects the ethnic structure of the Vitez Municipality that was under the control of the BiH army. So this is the area that we have been talking about just a moment ago and from which as we said 1,243 persons left. Of course, this population movement of the population under the control of the BiH army was unforced. There was a number of Serbs here who lived in Stolevic, about 150 of them, and they left this area even before 16th April, so in this chart we see the demographic structure of the population in 1995; that is after the changes which were brought about by the war. So in the first column, there is a number of Bosniaks who live in this area, and this is 8,282, or 95.92 per cent. The other columns reflects the number of Croats, so if we look at column number 3, there are only 25 Bosnian Croats remaining to reside in this area at the end of 1995. Then Bosnian Serbs, 7,274 Yugoslavs and 45 others. So the total at the end of 1995 is 8,634 inhabitants. The main characteristics of these changes as reflected in this chart are that this too is now also ethnically a pretty cleansed area, but there has been much less movement of population in the area controlled by the HVO. There was more than 6,000 who moved, whereas here it is only 1,243. Also the methods whereby people moved were different in the area controlled by the HVO. Part of the population moved voluntarily, like the Serbs, and in the -- and also some of the Croats moved because they were told to do so by the HVO. We also have the -- we see the bars here that reflect this mono-ethnic population in 1995. So this is just a graphic means of expressing the same numbers and we see that it is significant in this area as well, even though they were brought about by different means and they reflect different motives.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, I was just looking at the transcript. You indicated in the transcript that there was much less movement -- much less population movement in the areas controlled by the HVO. Did you mean the HVO or the areas controlled by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that in this area under the control of the army, 1,243 persons moved. This is in reference to the documents which we saw before, and that is a much lesser number, because in the other area, over 6,000 people moved, but the problem is not this. It is also an important fact, whether there is 5 people or 5,000 people, but the essence is that the population from the area controlled by the HVO were forced out, whereas in the area under the control of the BiH army they were not moved by force; in other words the population moved voluntarily, like the Serbs did, or the Croats who left certain areas by invitation of the HVO to move to the area under their control, and the other reason why some of the Croats left the area controlled by the BiH army was the pressure, but it was pressure on the basis of the military operations. I mentioned Poculica, I could have also mentioned part of Kruscica which is called Bobasi. That is where Croats lived and when the front-line moved, they had to withdraw from that area because of the combat operations that were taking place there. There was no daily pressure breaking into the homes to force them to move from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kajmovic. I am going to turn to a different area of your study. You mentioned earlier and you showed us a graphic that the Vitez Municipality was divided into 17 local communes. Many of those particular communes remained either exclusively in the territory controlled by the HVO or exclusively in the territory controlled by the ABiH, but some of those local communes were in fact divided by the confrontation lines; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would like to turn, if I could, to the fourth set of exhibits, which will be exhibits 202 through 205 which, Mr. Kajmovic, as you will shortly see are tables showing the population movements of the various ethnic groups within the local communes themselves, so if you would be so kind starting with exhibit 202 by placing that on the ELMO and explaining to the members of the Trial Chamber what this exhibit represents, and then we will go through the remaining other exhibits, 203 and 204 and 205. I appreciate it, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a document which compares the figures and it gives the comparison of the number of Bosniaks in 1991 as compared to the number in 1995. So we have the figures for each local commune, and the table tells us exactly how many Bosniaks were living in each local community in 1991 and how many of them were left in 1995. If we take for instance this first horizontal line, the number of Bosniaks living in Sadovaca local commune, there were 369 of them. Here is the percentage as compared to the total number of inhabitants of the local commune. Then we have the number of expelled Bosniaks by the end of the war, that is the end of 1995, and the number of Bosniaks that remained in 1995 were 380. This is the number of Bosniaks at the end of 1995, but we cannot see any expulsion of Bosniaks; in fact there are a few more of them than there were. This is because that part of the local commune remained under the control of the BiH army, whereas the part of the same local commune under the control of the HVO is inhabited by Bosnian Croats, so there was no shifting of the lines between the ethnic territories. In the local commune of Bukva, again we have no ethnic changes because it is a single ethnic communities inhabited by Bosniaks. In fact the number of inhabitants increased due to refugees coming from the area under the control of the HVO. Then the local commune of Lupac, again no changes because it is a Bosniak settlement, Preocica the same; Stare Bila, we have a change. For instance there were 2,929 Bosniaks living there in 1991 and at the end of 1995, we see the figure zero, which means that all 2,929 of them had been expelled. Then the local commune of Jardol, there used to be 743 Bosniaks living there in 1991. At the end of 1995, there are none; they were all expelled. Then the local commune of Krcevine in 1991 and it is under HVO control. This local commune, there were 173 Bosniaks, and we see the figure of 134, which means somewhat less than before, but this is due to the fact that the northern part of that local commune remains under the BiH army control, so the Bosniaks stayed on there. In Dubravica, we have the number of Bosniaks, 447; then somewhat less, 358. There are fewer of them because a part of that local commune was under the control of the HVO, and that is why the total number is smaller because the local commune has been cut in half, so they have remained in the area under the army control, whereas the area under HVO control there are none. Then the local commune of 25th May there were 471 Bosniaks. We see there are 316 of them now, which is somewhat less. Again the same applies to this local commune, because it was cut in half. The area under army control has retained its Bosniak population, whereas the area under HVO control has none. Then Ahmici, it is a specific case. In 1991, there were 506 Bosniaks living there, 508, and here we see that there are none left. There are no Bosniaks left there, because they were expelled in the first two days of the fighting, 16th and 17th April, and, of course, 117 people were killed. The local commune of Poculica, with respect to Bosniaks, there were no population changes because it remained under the control of the army; in fact we have an increase of the number of Bosniaks due to people coming over from other areas. Then we have significant changes in the local communes of Vitez 1 and Vitez 2, which are dealt with jointly in this table, and we see that there were about 2,647 Bosniaks living there, that there are now 1,166, which means that about 1,500 have been expelled, which is from the part of the town that is under HVO control. They have remained in that small part called Stari Vitez which remains under the control of the BiH army. Then the local commune of Rijeka; here we have some minor changes in the population. We will be able to see later what those changes are. A part of this local commune also remained under the control of the army and a part under the HVO control, so that the population was expelled from the part under the HVO control, though a small percentage did remain as part of those 80 people I mentioned. Then the local commune of Kruscica, there were no significant changes with respect to the Bosniak population. That local commune is also divided by the separation line; a part is under the control of the army, a part under the HVO, and that is why there are no major changes. Then the local commune of Gacice, in the first line we see there were 325 Bosniaks and in the third column, we see a zero, which means all the Bosniaks were expelled from this local commune, because the HVO captured this local commune, the local commune of Gacice. Veceriska, first we see there were 388 Bosniaks; in the third line we see none, so this is another local commune captured by the HVO for three days, during the first few days of the conflict, and we have no Bosniaks there left. So there were a total of 11,514 Bosniaks in 1991, and at the end of 1995, there are 8,352 of them. That is the reduction due to so-called ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, now could you turn to exhibits 203, 204 and 205 and, without going into such detail, can you just briefly explain if those charts likewise compare the data between 1991 and 1995 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon. I have to come in at this point. Obviously you cannot summarise months and months of studies, and we want to congratulate the witness for having done that, but we would like to see you explain the method, explain the other charts. Just start with the totals. Discuss the results of the research and point out those points which you think are the most important, such as the village of Sadovaca, where there was a correlation with the first chart you referred to. We do not want to spend the entire afternoon with these charts. You did explain the issue of demographic changes, it has been explained well, and now let us try to synthesise the work that has been done. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, then for the record, the remaining charts which are exhibits 203, 204 and 205 are like comparative studies done in respect of the ethnic populations of Croats, Serbs and others in the various local communes in the Vitez municipality, comparing the data from 1991 to 1995. If the court desires, after taking a look at these exhibits briefly, any explanation from Mr. Kajmovic, he is prepared to expand further on those; otherwise we will turn to our additional set of exhibits, our last sets of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like the witness to explain something. We are not going to go from one extreme to another. I would like the witness to explain for the other three charts the general idea. If there are any specific comments that he wants to make, let him make them, but in general terms, this is what the judges would like the witness to do. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a summary. The substance, the aim was, as this is a case study in terms of research, this is considered a case study, and then one is able to enter into the details at greater length, so I try to establish at the micro level what the actual changes were in each local commune and inhabited places. I believe that there are a lot of figures and data involved, so I think that we will not lose too much time if we go on to these last exhibits which show the final outcome of the ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I think that we could now move to another series of questions. It is almost self-evident, Mr. Harmon. If later the

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: or that figure, we would then go back to the details, but I think that if everybody agrees about the general sense of the testimony, we could move to another question. You must decide what is the best to do now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Fine, thank you, Mr. President. If I could have the assistance of the usher and move to my final two exhibits, which are 206 and 207. This will put into focus the demographic changes in the whole of the Vitez Municipality, that is both areas, those areas controlled by the HVO and those areas controlled by the ABiH, and it will indicate the data in 1995. These obviously, Mr. President, can be compared with exhibits 193 and 194, which show the baseline data in 1991. If I could have Mr. Kajmovic start with exhibit 206, which is a table and a graph, and if the table itself could be put into sharp focus, Mr. Kajmovic can start with the table itself, and then turn to the graph that is associated with it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here we have a table showing the ethnic composition of the population of Vitez Municipality at the end of 1995; that is the ethnic composition that was the result of the war and of the ethnic cleansing. The first column gives us the number of Bosnian Croats. There were 15,246 of them as compared to 1991. We see that their number has increased by about 2,500. Then the number of Bosniaks, 8,362, as compared to 11,500, their number has gone down; the number of Serbs 107, as compared to 1,501 in 1991, again a drastic reduction; among the Yugoslavs, 1,377, there are 918 left; as for others, their number has gone down from about 790 to 301, and finally we have the total population which is 24,934, and we know that Vitez Municipality, at the end of 1991, had close to 28,000 inhabitants. So here we have the collective figures of the ethnic structure, but the main goal of this table is not to show how much one ethnic group has decreased or another increased in number, but rather to show the zeros which show how extreme the ethnic cleansing was. So, compared with the table for 1991, you will rarely in that table find a zero for any ethnic group in hardly any local commune, but here you will see quite a large number of those zeros, though this cannot be seen from this table, but the parts of local communes under the control of the HVO are completely without other inhabitants. But this cannot be seen from this table, in the case of local communes that were divided, but there is an obvious drastic change in the population structure. Then we have a graph, a bar chart, reflecting the composition of the population in 1995, and you can see that 61.14 per cent are Croats, whereas in 1991, they constituted 45 per cent of the total, which means their share has increased by more than 16 per cent. There were 41 per cent Bosniaks, there are 33.53 per cent of them now, so that their number has gone down by about 7 or 8 per cent; the number of Serbs has also drastically decreased, but I must note that they left the area voluntarily. The number of Yugoslavs has gone down, but not to such an extent, and the number of others has also gone down, though not to the same extent as in the case of Bosniaks and Serbs. Those are the consequences of the ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE WERE TO
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, could you then turn to the last exhibit which is exhibit 207, a map with various coloured dots. Could you explain to the Trial Chamber what this particular exhibit represents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning, we had a similar ethnic map which showed the distribution of the population in Vitez Municipality in 1991. Now we have another map showing how that population is ethnically distributed within the territory of Vitez Municipality. Comparing it with the first map, we can see that in this area which is under the control of the HVO, we have mostly blue dots, which stand for the percentage share of the Croats, and here we see the percentage that they constitute 61 per cent, so we have 61 of these blue dots showing how those Bosnian Croats are distributed in this area. In this other part, in this other segment, we have these green dots, as well as up here, (indicates) which show that there are Bosniaks living there, and the number of dots is indicative of their percentage share, which is about 33 per cent. Here in this small circle which covers the territory of Stari Vitez, it shows us the percentage share of the population living there. There are -- the substance of this table is a review of the changes that have occurred in the distribution of the population. So we have a significant departure from the previous distribution of the population, that is in 1991. So these are the figures that we have already mentioned, 6,000 and something inhabitants moved out of this part, whereas from these two parts 1,200 were displaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kajmovic. Mr. President, I would now move into evidence Prosecution exhibits 192 through to 207. I have concluded my examination of Mr. Kajmovic, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now take a break for 30 minutes. (4.20 pm) (A short break) (5.00 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will resume the hearing now, please have the accused brought in. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will begin with the cross-examination of the witness. Let me remind you that we are going to sit today until 7.00. Mr. Nobilo, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Mr. Kajmovic, good evening. As you heard, I am Anto Nobilo and together with Russell Hayman, my colleague, we represent General Blaskic and I am going to ask you a few questions. Has your work been published anywhere?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness's microphone is not on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the paper has not been published yet. There is a plan to defend it in June or July, in front of the committee at the Political Science School in Sarajevo. There will be three PhD members of this committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Have you provided the Prosecution either an outline of your thesis or any tables?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only the part concerning demographic changes which were relevant for this topic were provided to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This is what you gave to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we do not want any delay, and we will continue with the cross-examination, but I would just like to notify you that Mr. Kajmovic has been -- that we were notified of Mr. Kajmovic's testimony several months ago. We know him as a member of the Bosniak party. He is one of the key figures concerning the conflict there, but only on Friday did we receive the information that Dr. Kajmovic would be called as an expert witness, and we received absolutely no accompanying documents. We feel that it was necessary for you to know this, but we will continue the cross-examination anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You did not even get the charts, the tables? You did not get any of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Nothing, your Honour, nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, under a court order that both Defence counsel and the Prosecutor understood, and have corresponded about in the past, it is our understanding that expert reports are not discoverable. That is based on a court order of this chamber issued many, many, many months ago. In the course of the subsequent conversations with counsel, we have had a dialogue in writing, in part, about that decision. I can provide a copy to the court of correspondence, but that has been our understanding, and we have operated on that in good faith.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: May I state our position?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I am looking at things on a somewhat different level. I think there are two issues here. The issue was brought in because of his position in the SDA, that is the first problem, but the second one is to do with what I would like to focus the debate on, which has to do with the expert report, which you cannot say really is a report because it has not been given as a report officially. I am referring to these charts, and I understand it is not easy to cross-examine if you base yourself only on charts. That is what I find a bit surprising, because when we think about it from the point of view of an adversarial system, the report should have been at least made available to the Defence or if not made available, that they would have been informed about it. There should have been a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I received the tables myself this weekend when I started talking to Mr. Kajmovic. We were aware of the existence of those -- before this weekend, not just this weekend. The tables were not translated before the weekend. I have been working with them in order to get them in a form that I and your Honours would understand in order that they could be presented today. However, to answer your question directly, Mr. President, the charts were not turned over to counsel. When we concluded we would be having him testify about reports he brought with him from Bosnia to here, we informed counsel, but it took some time for me to review and understand those, but they have not been provided to counsel, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, do you want to comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Please. Our position as to this witness, your Honour, is that his Master's thesis and any drafts of that thesis are not in the nature of an expert report, but are his statements. Even if it is a draft, it is still written by the witness, it is in his hand, and if any portions of that thesis have been provided to the Prosecutor, they were owed to the Defence as prior statements of the witness. I agree with Mr. Harmon that the court's earlier order did not direct the production of expert reports by the Prosecutor. Although we think that that would be a good idea, that is not the way the rules are in the system I am familiar with, where statements of experts are normally produced, but with respect to this witness, we are not raising that issue, we are simply suggesting that portions of his thesis were statements and that it would have facilitated things had we gotten them. But we wish to proceed; we do not wish to delay the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I clarify one point? That is the report, so it is perfectly clear for the record, any reports that Mr. Kajmovic had accompanying the tables were not in a language I understood, nor have they ever been translated by me. These tables and charts when I discussed the issues with Mr. Kajmovic were the tables and charts that he had contained in his study that would illuminate his efforts to assess the demographic changes. When we concluded that that would be an area of expert testimony, given the fact that there probably are very few people in the world who have studied the ethnic demographic changes in Vitez Municipality under what are extremely difficult circumstances, we concluded that he is -- would be an expert in the area. We notified counsel of that and I can say very honestly to this court, Mr. President, the reports that he has that accompany those tables and charts I have never read.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, we understand the situation. However, you need to know that for months, we have been misled. For months we have looked at Mr. Munib Kajmovic as a key figure in the international conflict. He was the President of the SDA and led the efforts of the SDA during the conflict, and now we find out that he is an expert. Had we known that he would be called as an expert, that is how we would have prepared our cross-examination, and that would have been our preparation for this hearing. But again, we are prepared to continue, nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nobilo and Mr. Harmon. While you were speaking, I was able to consult with my colleagues very quickly. As regards the first point, that having to do with the surprise you expressed that he is not testifying about that area about which he said he was an expert before that, that is not something that we can do anything about. We cannot do anything about that, because that was the strategy of the Prosecutor. However in order to ensure equitable treatment, my colleagues want me to speak for them and to say that if, confronted with these charts which are complicated and which would require possibly a thorough review, if at any point you would like to have this witness brought back again, the Tribunal will grant that wish and it can be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We will try to conduct the cross-examination, but if at the end of the cross-examination we determine that we have not illuminated all the details, we will request that the witness be recalled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Then we agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kajmovic, your mentor, Mr. Mirko Pejanovic, what is the area of his expertise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are various subjects from the area of political science and I do not know exactly what topic he covers, because he was appointed to it by the faculty, but I think he covers various areas. For instance, he probably is a lecturer in the methodology, the social system, interest groups, so I do not know exactly what subject he is lecturing in right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What exactly is the title of your MA thesis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Political and demographic changes in the Vitez Municipality between 1992 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you conducted consultations about this thesis, was it agreed that you would reflect the demographic changes in numbers and statistics, or did you also agree on researching the causes of demographic movements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was specified which aspects would be treated. The historical aspect from the Turkish era to Austro-Hungary and pre-World War II and the modern time, then there will be an economic aspect, the economic development part, then the administrative territorial position of the Vitez Municipality; then the elections of 1990, so all this is contained in the thesis. Then there will be combat operations in the area from 16th April 1993 to 25th February 1994, and also it was indicated that the demographic changes would be covered as a result of the war efforts and the ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What I am interested in is that in your thesis, was the agreement also made that the causes, the root causes, of the population movements will also be treated; is that what is written there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but only the demographic changes, but if you do not go into the causes scientifically, it is not a valid thesis, so you have to go to the causes of these movements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. Let us go to the causes of these demographic changes. What scientific method did you use to determine the causes of demographic changes in the Vitez Municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This probably can be viewed from two standpoints, purely theoretical, looking at it from the political point of view, reflecting global political interests and more locally, or what changes followed these global political motives, so the changes on the ground. These two aspects have to be combined and the causes cannot be looked for on a purely local level, so you have to look at the general or global political changes that were taking place in Bosnia in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Okay, from the global and local points of view. How did you proceed? What did you look for when you were looking for causes of the population movements? What specifically did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When speaking of the causes, we know what happened on the ground, and when now you try to find a theoretical foundation for it, when you try to explain why this happened, you have to start from a wider point of view, both in terms of the time period and the geography. You have to see where the policy of the HVO was created, who was involved and what was the final goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, in your response, you said, "we know what happened". As a scholar, for the purposes of your work, did you go to research what happened or you used your previous knowledge as the President of the SDA in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I worked on the ground and I used documents to support my thesis of what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This is precisely my question. What was it that you were looking for, what documents were you looking at and how did your research on the ground look?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As concerning documents, I used the documents by the Civilian Defence Headquarters in Vitez. Then I used Red Cross Vitez documents, and Merhamet documents, and the local commune services of the Vitez Municipality documents and what was most important for me, it was the interviews with persons who were expelled and people who went in the field, so that was the research in the field. So the research in the field and the interviews helped me to confirm the data from the documents which I received from institutions like the census of the Bosnia area which was conducted by the Civilian Defence Headquarters in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, now we are talking about your research of the causes of the population movements. In the documents of the Civilian Defence Headquarters in Vitez, and I presume that this is the headquarters of the Bosniak side, as well as the Merhamet documents, the Red Cross documents and others, are there statistical data there or are there causes also addressed there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just the data, and I did that to compare it to see what were the causes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. Let us then focus on the interviews. What method of finding the right sample did you use? In other words, how did you go about selecting the persons that you interviewed? Was it random sample or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With interviews, I used the principle that from each area from where people were expelled, that would be the Ahmici, Jardol, which includes Grbavica, Veceriska, Gacice and Vitez 1 local communes, so I knew the areas from which the people were expelled, so I used random samples and I interviewed a certain number of people there and then I summed up the results and I arrived at the ways and means by which these people were forced out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How many people did you interview from these five local communes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I conducted about 40 to 50 interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was it evenly spread out over the communes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How many men, how many women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I paid attention that the age groups be represented, so I took care to interview some younger people, older people and some women, so I did take that into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: When you speak to one another, it is best to turn off your microphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When analysing these statements, did you ask your investigators if you used them or did you set out in advance that you would take this many women or men or was it random?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not random. I know what the interviews are, I know what the survey is, I know what the historical methods are of using the scientific methods, I had to adjust, so it is not my own personal wish which led me to this result.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In these interviews, Mr. Kajmovic, did you come across for instance the cases for instance from Gacice, a population left under the protection of the international forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
