utterances.text: Yes, I have certain data reflecting that for Gacice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know and did you come across this in the interviews, that after two days of fighting in Donje Veceriska, the military left, together with the population, in an organised manner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a fact that a few people who had some weapons there pulled back together with the population, but, militarily speaking, this was not any significant organised military force.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Next question. Do you know that the civilian population of Donje Veceriska withdrew together with those few people with weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Before the HVO came to where they were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The HVO attacked Donje Veceriska, and after this attack, the population withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Together with those few people under arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, together with those few people who had some arms; that is the information I obtained.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know that UNPROFOR participated in this operation, in moving out the population from Donje Veceriska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not familiar with those details.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Regarding Grbavica, Jardol, the local commune, do you know that again the inhabitants left Grbavica under protection and in an organised fashion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is out of the question. The inhabitants of Grbavica at the beginning of September, I think it was 4th or 5th September, after the line was broken through, the front-line, the population pulled out, at least the few that were there while the lines were intact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So when the front-line was broken through, the Bosnian army was broken through, a part of the population pulled out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a part of the population pulled out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In your view, regarding Grbavica for example, did the population of Grbavica withdraw because of combat operation, because the army belonging to that population was losing its positions on the front, or because flats were broken into and the people were exposed to force and violence? What is the reason for the withdrawal of the population of Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The case of Grbavica is to some extent rather specific. A part of the population in that locality, due to combat operations, was withdrawn, but a part remained, and after the line fell, a smaller section withdrew, but for instance 1,500 inhabitants of the local commune Vitez 1, or Vitez 2, that is the town of Vitez proper, were entirely surrounded and they had to leave the town under pressure through various forms of coercion. The same happened to the inhabitants of Veceriska, also Gacice, also the inhabitants of the local commune of Ahmici. Therefore we have a slightly different situation in this case, which could perhaps compare with a part of Bobasi, the local commune of Kruscica inhabited by Croats, where the population also had to withdraw because the front-line changed, but viewed globally, these ethnic displacements were large, and these were peripheral cases, because on the whole, this was systematic ethnic cleansing. There are always certain exceptions to the rule and there is no doubt about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Regarding what happened in Grbavica, according to your research, in Grbavica, Donje Veceriska and Gacice, is it similar or different to what happened in Vitez 1 and 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are certain differences. To be specific, in Donje Veceriska, the inhabitants after a night and a day pulled out facing the attack of the HVO, whereas in Vitez, the town itself, which was under HVO control, there were no combat operations. The 1,500 Bosniaks in the city centre were actually contained within that centre and there was nowhere they could go, and then pressure was brought to bear on them and they were expelled, whereas in the case of Veceriska, the HVO gave them some space, a way out, so to speak, that they could go through to reach the line behind which the BiH army had control. Of course, a certain number of civilians were killed in the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have the exact figure, but I think up to about ten women and men were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So have I understood you well: when you say that the situation in the town of Vitez was one and the situation in the villages was a different one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In principle, there is no difference. The Bosniak population of Veceriska would never have left that area if it had not been for the HVO attacks on that local commune. As regards the town of Vitez itself, 1,500 Bosniaks of Vitez would never have left that part of town, even though the HVO did not attack it, because it already had it under its control before then, the people would not have left. I am one of the inhabitants of the town of Vitez, my house that I built for 16 years, it is across the road from the secondary school, and many other people like me who live there abandoned it and were expelled from that area. Therefore from the point of view of the principle, the principle is force. They left this area under pressure of force, under coercion. That is the basic principle. Whether it was expressed in this or that way with certain shades of differences, certain nuances, the principle remains the same. Behind the displacement of the population, there was force and nothing else, when we are talking about the area under HVO control.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Are war operations a force? Is that coercion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course a war is coercion. The HVO attack is a force. If somebody is attacking you with arms, you have to flee your home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In your research, did you study the documents of the International Red Cross or the Vitez Municipality, and I mean the part of the municipality under control of the Croats, and from these documents, it would follow that under the control of the International Red Cross, all the people who left Vitez made a statement saying that they were doing so voluntarily and that they had chosen the place they were going to themselves. Have you seen those documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not seen the Red Cross documents, but I have seen some UNHCR documents, containing certain statistical reports on the number of inhabitants, the number of exiles and the number who lived there and these are quite inaccurate, because those data were given to them by both the Croatian and the Bosniak sides, and they exaggerated them by about 50 per cent, so as to get a little more humanitarian aid. That is why the UNHCR data are quite incorrect. As for the statements given by the displaced persons to the Red Cross, I have not had any insight into them, but through my interviews, I learnt some things. The HVO is in the town centre where the municipal library is and an office was organised there, to which the Bosniaks would come and they had to sign documents there saying that they were moving out voluntarily and that they -- they even had to exchange apartments. Of course, under wartime conditions that were very risky, people sought to get out at all cost, from that environment. A better description would be to say to escape from hell. When they had to go to the Zenica Municipality, to move into a Croatian flat, there was not recognised, of course, that people were manipulated by the HVO and that was how this area was ethnically cleansed. Therefore I am quite familiar with this and I think that the statements collected by the HVO and that may have been given to the Red Cross under those circumstances are irrelevant, because the statements would surely be quite different if they were not exposed to the same kind of risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Are you aware of the documents made under the supervision of the Red Cross in Vitez, when people were leaving the school at Dubravica, the cinema hall et cetera; have you seen those documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not seen those documents, but I know that a certain number of people were detained in the Workers' University, which was a camp; also another group of people opposite that camp across the way in the SDK social accounting service building, I know that when Sefer Halilovic came and signed the cease-fire, when he arrived at the Workers' University and arranged with the HVO authorities that a certain number be released that at the time 12 to 15 people were taken to Busovaca, so I am aware of all these details. But what I wish to underline here is that the statements and the certificates, decisions signed in the library in Vitez under the HVO auspices are irrelevant, and that they give you quite a different picture from what those same people would tell you now. Their main motive, their main wish is to get out and save their lives, because a certain number of people were killed there, a certain number of Bosniaks were killed within those areas, that is the areas under HVO control before 16th April. So no BiH army representatives were there at the time, so they sought to get out in whatever way they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So will you agree with me that it follows from everything that you have said that your only source of information regarding the causes of departure from the Municipality of Vitez were interviews, and that you did not have insight into all the documents of the Red Cross and the authorities in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Red Cross data mainly say whether somebody was detained, that he was a prisoner, that after that, he received a booklet which proves that he was a detainee, and in this decision or this booklet, you cannot find anything except what I have just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So you did not see the document in which a citizen gives a statement where he wishes to go and that he is going voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not seen those documents, but I know from my method of interviews that people were asked, "Do you want to go to Travnik or do you want to go to Zenica?" But one could ask a different question, why was such a question put to those people? Who are the people who are ready to leave their homes and then somebody would ask them, "Where is it you want to go?"

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You have just explained your method regarding the Bosniaks. Will you please tell me, did you respect the basic principles of science -- were the same principles applied when interviewing Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. In view of the fact that the political situation over there is what it is, it is theoretically unfeasible for me to go there and carry out research, even to have this method of interviews, so I point out in my thesis that this part of the data were obtained by estimates, using auxiliary data, so that when talking about the paper as a whole, then these demographic changes are quite precise with respect to one segment, and when it comes to the Croatian segment, there may be certain deviations, as I said, of 5 to 6 per cent. They cannot be more than that, so that these data may also be accepted as being correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You have not understood me. My question was, what was your method for establishing the reasons for the departure of Croats? Did you use the same methods among Croats and Serbs to establish why those people left their homes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not possible for me to do any kind of research in the area under HVO control, because the Bosniaks have been expelled from those parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I apologise, but please listen to me. My question is: did you interview the Croats who fled from territories under control of the BiH army? Did you interview them to see why they had fled their homes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since this applies to some 900 Croats, since I am aware of the case of Croats in Stari Vitez, I did not conduct interviews, but I pointed out those few cases. There are about 400 Croats who were living in the local commune of Poculica who, on 16th April, in the morning, the first day when the HVO did not manage to gain control of that particular local commune, they left that area together with HVO members, so this was almost half of the Croats that were moved, and the other half of Croats who were displaced are the Croats in the local commune of Kruscica in Bobasi, who during combat operations later on, when the front-line was moved, they withdrew within the territory under HVO control. Therefore the changes that occurred among the Croats happened practically in the first couple of days, and, of course, a certain percentage of Croats withdrew that night, so logic says that they must have been informed by the HVO to cross over to territory under their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let me put the same question differently. In your research, when establishing the causes for the fleeing of Croats from their homes in the territories under BiH army command, did you use any scientific methods or did you use your knowledge while you were President of the SDA in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My role has --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, let me have a chance to object. I object, Mr. President. The question has been asked and answered about three or four times. Mr. Kajmovic has explained why he could not do research and how he conducted his investigation in respect of displaced Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, sustained. Change questions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You mentioned the case of Croats moving when the front-line changed. Is that according to ethnic cleansing, or is it movement due to combat operations? How would you define it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the specific case of Bobasi, then one could apply the reasoning that it was due to a change in the front-line in the case of Croats, and the same applies to Grbavica where the Bosniaks were displaced because of a change in the front-line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, with respect to the movement of Croats from the territory under BiH army control, was that influenced by the fact that in Krizancevo Selo, the BiH army killed 74 civilians, in Buhine Kuce 30, in Sadovaca another 30. Were those facts established according to you and did this influence the displacement of Croats from the territory under BiH army control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A part of the analysis has been left out. In that part of the analysis, reference is made to the consequences of the war or rather the HVO aggression against the Bosniaks of Vitez. I have only analysed briefly a table showing that 4,000 and something Bosniaks were expelled,, that some went to Zenica, some to Travnik and some went abroad. We left out the part dealing with the 3,514 Bosniaks killed. We left that part out. I investigated that matter and, regarding the number of Croats killed, of course, I only have certain estimates for that. My estimates show that the number is not small, that a large number of people were killed, but this case that Mr. Nobilo is mentioning, Bobasi, Krizancevo Selo, those are classical combat operations between the army and the HVO conducted during the war, and there were certain minor changes in the front-line to one side or the other, so this was a traditional clash between two armies. So one cannot talk about the suffering of civilians in this case, as for instance when the army captured a certain territory and conducted a massacre. That is not true, Krizancevo Selo remained under HVO control, and a part of Buhine Kuce also remained under HVO control.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Have I understood you well? Does it follow from what you have said that these 74 people, inhabitants of Krizancevo Selo and Buhine Kuce, the 30, that they were not killed outside combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, those were mostly HVO soldiers, and I think that you are familiar with the report of UNPROFOR. UNPROFOR was there, who filmed it. These are well known facts, established facts, that they were HVO soldiers. Maybe in some cases a couple of civilians, I am not sure, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you establish during your research what percentage of the territory since the Washington treaty is controlled by the BiH army and which percentage of the Vitez Municipality by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, HVO controls 25 per cent and the BiH army 75 per cent, but half of the Vitez Municipality of 1,599 square kilometres is not inhabited. These are woods and hills. The parts under HVO control are all the communications, the town centres, with the exception of 5.3 square kilometres within Vitez itself. All the work enterprises, the educational institutions et cetera are within the control of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I were to say that the HVO controlled the settlements along communication lines and the vital economic establishments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you referring to April 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No, during the Muslim/Croat war. Would you agree with that definition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on 25th February 1994, the Washington treaty came into force and the armies were separated and it was then that they gained control of 25 per cent, with the coming into force of the truce.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You may not have understood me. Those 25 per cent under HVO control, after the signing of the truce; can it be defined as covering settlements along major communications and the key economic facilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: During your research, did you establish how many Muslim refugees came to the Vitez Municipality from eastern Bosnia and how many from Jajce before the Croatian-Muslim conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a question I have studied and, since we left out that part of the statistics, the total number of Bosniak refugees at the end of 1995 within Vitez under BiH army control amounts to 331, I think. I should have to look it up. So it is a very small number of refugees. There were not many Bosniak refugees from other areas within the territory of Vitez Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said -- you gave us the figure for 1995, but do you have the figure for 1993? There were refugees coming in in 1992. I am asking you, before the Muslim-Croat war, how many refugees were there in Vitez Municipality from Jajce and eastern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a very interesting question from a slightly different angle. I have not established the exact number, though I did study it from a different standpoint. A large number of the refugees came from western parts of Bosnia, they reached Travnik and they went on to look for shelter. Throughout that time, the HVO government of Vitez did its best to prevent a large number of Bosniaks from staying in Vitez Municipality. At the time, I was not aware of the reasons, though they frequently mentioned the need not to upset the ethnic mix. Therefore at the beginning of 1993, Vitez Municipality, as compared to Zenica or Travnik, there was a very small percentage of Bosniak refugees. Anyway, you see how many there were at the end of the war, 300 and something.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Have I understood you well; you are not aware of the number of refugees in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, but if there were many of them, they would have still been there at the end of 1995. There would have been more than 300 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In the course of your research, did you analyse the situation in the surrounding municipalities, and did those events affect the demographic situation in Vitez? Do you know how many Croats came from Zenica, Travnik, Novi Travnik and Busovaca to the Vitez Municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a case study, so that you are dealing with a legal problem which has to be studied. Therefore no further elaborations were made regarding other municipalities, but the statistical data shows that the number of Croats in Vitez Municipality increased by about 2,500 at the end of 1995, as compared to the 1991 census, so those Croats must have come from somewhere, and mostly they came from Travnik and a certain number, I do not know the exact number, from Zenica. Whether there were a few coming from Vares or some other places like Fojnica, but it is a fact that there were 2,500 of them more than before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you not think it was important to investigate this? Let me ask you a question. Do you know how many autochthonous Croats left Vitez Municipality in spite of HVO control? Do you have those figures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The number could only be quite negligible for this study, because at the end of 1992, and in the course of 1992 even, there were some small -- a small degree of mobility because in that situation of uncertainty, both Bosniaks and Croats were leaving, going to Croatia, but many of them came back, so that this percentage, how many there were, would not substantively change the demographic situation in Vitez Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But did you use any precise methods to establish how many Croats had left Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When you are doing demographic changes, you have to bear in mind that these are living people. You may establish the population structure one day and already the next day it will be somewhat changed, so it is not possible to approach the problem in that way. You have the birth rate, the death rate, the natural increment, the moving out of people for reasons of employment, and for other reasons, for educational purposes et cetera. So it is not possible to establish each individual case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, if I adduce from what you have said that you needed to establish how many members of a particular ethnic group moved, but you did not establish how many Croats came from Zenica, how many Croats who had lived in Vitez had left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The fact that is relevant is the number of Croats in Vitez Municipality today as compared to the 1991 census.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So you did not come across the figure that 500 military conscripts of the HVO had left Vitez? These are young people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do not know whether you investigated how many fighters were killed during the combat operations and who is responsible for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: 2,100 in the Municipality of Vitez, 700, in the whole enclave, 2,100 Croats were killed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, in my paper I mention the figure of 700.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know the 20,000 Croats from Travnik before the April conflict came to the Vitez Municipality; they were expelled from Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I am aware, the largest number of Croats from Travnik, though I did not study this very seriously, went across the lines held by the Chetniks, across Mount Vlasik, and a part of the Croats came to Vitez Municipality, that is in the area where there were combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know that 5,000 Croats from Zenica abandoned Zenica and came to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of these figures, so I would not like to answer questions that I have not studied in my paper and for which I do not have reliable data.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I do not know what you have studied and that is why I am asking you. Do you know that all the Croats of Fojnica left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know -- I have said that I studied, that I did a case study devoted to Vitez Municipality and my theme does not involve studying the surroundings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But I am talking about the people of Fojnica who came to Vitez Municipality?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me object because the questions and answers are merging into one. I think there should be some pause to allow the translation from Mr. Nobilo and some time for Mr. Kajmovic to answer and let his answer be translated before the next question is asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think this is an objection to which everybody would agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I will attempt -- I just got carried away a little bit. Sorry. Mr. Kajmovic, you are a scholar, so let me just try to confirm something with you. What does it seem to you when you use Bosnian Croat and Bosnian Serb? Is that a scientific term or is this a political term? Is this a new nation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The correct denomination for Croats would be the Bosnian Croat, because it is the Croats who live in Bosnia, in the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina and not in the state of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is that a scientific name of a nation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The correct name is Croats, only Croats, but I stress the prefix Bosnian, so that we would distinguish between the Croats who live in Croatia and those who live in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so we know about which Croats we were talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did any Croats from Croatia move to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you use the term Serbian Bosniaks for people from Sandzak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not dealing in that issue at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But have you ever heard it, Serbian Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in real life.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Would you not agree that this is a little bit ridiculous?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, why?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. We go back to 1995, when you were trying to determine how many people of which ethnic group lived, resided in which area of the Municipality. Let us take the Bosniaks for instance. Was this a scientific method?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the Civilian Defence Headquarters did hire people to canvass the neighbourhoods and so they did it for their own purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What method did you use when determining the number of Bosniaks in the territory under the HVO control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here I used the method of interviews, so the interviews with people who knew their neighbours in Rijeka, because we took Rijeka, that is part of the Vranska local commune, part of it is in Rijeka, part of it is in Vitez too, so I knew Bosniaks there who knew their neighbours very well and so I interviewed people from the Vitez too, the urban part of the area, who had left there but knew exactly who stayed behind. So that we had those two cases, the 80 Bosniaks in the urban part of Vitez, and part in Rijeka, so that was a small area which was specifically researched.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was this a scientific method?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, this is accurate, it is 80 people who were registered there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you look at other settlements, whether there were Bosniaks there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not. By talking to people who were going to these areas, who went to check on their own houses, who went to the cemeteries, and so we identified exactly how many Bosniaks were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How scientifically reliable is this that you have just described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The most precise would be if the census bureau of Bosnia would be able to go into the field and identify these 80 persons. It is not practicable right now, but these data are quite relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In your examination-in-chief, you explained that people who went to the cemeteries looked at how many houses were still standing and that is how you proceeded. What was the UNPROFOR's role in this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the first period after the cessation of hostilities, there was an agreement with UNPROFOR to provide escort and safety and later this was done between the HVO police and the Army of BiH and later people had more freedom of movement in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that in most cases, people were going in buses in an organised way to the cemeteries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part, but there were some individual cases as well, people who went there by themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did I understand correctly that when these people went on buses, they were counting Croatian houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they first went there, they were not in a position to. Later, yes, but they were not counting Croatian houses, they were counting their own houses, how many were destroyed et cetera and their neighbours; they were not interested in the Croatian houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But you said Croatian house times 3.7?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Bosniak houses. We know that about -- there were about 100, 40 were destroyed, 60 were moved in by other people, so I took the average number of family members for 89/90/91. The average number of members of family in the Vitez Municipality per family was 3.75, so if 60 houses were vacated and other people moved in, I would take that number 60 and multiply it by 3.75 and this is how I would come to the number of the Croats who have now moved and were residing in Donje Veceriska. I may be off by a certain percentage point, but not much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: One more question. What scientific method did you use to determine why the Serbs left? How did you determine that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbs are a separate case. Before the conflict, for the most part, most of them left voluntarily. There were 377 in the Vitez area, so a relatively small number in the municipality. In Tolovici, they had about 150 inhabitants. It was half Bosniak, half Serbian settlement. The rest of the Serbs were distributed in the urban area and some in Kruscica and some in Rijeka. I know this because I communicated with the Serbs at that time, and this is what they were saying, that Radovan Karadzic requested they leave this area, and they found buses and in an organised way they moved out before the conflict, for the most part. A small percentage stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Am I correct in saying here that this fact was determined by your previous knowledge and not based on your scientific research?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The knowledge that you possess, you cannot absolutely disregard and again come to it later. These are the facts that will be confirmed by all your collaborators, that is in respect of the Serbs. So all Croats will confirm this, it is not just the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But would it not have been fair to have asked the Serbs about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is reasoning for that too, but then maybe you should ask Karadzic who ordered this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In one of the tables, and I am talking to 5 to 6 percentage point deviation, could that be up and down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I say 5 to 6. I think it could go down by that amount, but maybe a little bit upward as well, but for the most part, it would be minus, that is down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In one of the tables, you showed the population chart in the areas under the HVO control in 1995, and you compared it to 1991. Certain local communes were split, and divided in certain ways. I would like to know whether you had data from 1991, how many Croats and how many Bosniaks lived in this segment of the area that is now under different controls?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was an Official Gazette, a local municipal Official Gazette. There are 34 inhabited places and in 1991, there was a census in these inhabited places. It was accurately determined how many inhabited places belonged in certain local communes, so in Lupac, for instance, you had 98 per cent of Bosniaks living. Let us take Jardol. Grbavica is part of that local commune, with some 700 Bosniaks, and I would have to look how many Croats there are there, so there are accurate data, so there is nothing controvertible there. We know exactly how many inhabitants of each ethnic group there is in which local commune, so in Jardol, in Grbavica et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you, as a scholar, as a scientist, the data that you put forward here which I cannot confirm right now that the Croats were in the majority of 93.8 per cent in the areas controlled by the HVO, and the Bosniaks 95.8, almost 96 per cent in the majority in the areas under BH control, so was it -- can you tell me, is the propaganda stronger or the force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do not tie it into either, please. There are accurate data here. In the area controlled by the BiH army, you can take the statistical data and compare. In Lupac, 400 people, only Bosniaks -- for instance Sadovaca, exclusively Bosniaks, that is the area controlled by the BiH army. Take the local commune of Vrhovine, exclusively Bosniak. Preocica, I think there were only 11 Croats there and maybe about the same number of Serbs. The local commune of Prnjavor, exclusively -- Vrhovine, exclusively Bosniaks. This can be gleaned through other tables as well, so there was -- the areas under the BiH army control were much less mixed, but the ones that are now under HVO control was much more mixed. It was flat, it was industrially more developed et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Okay. Do you agree that the territory under the BiH army control was ethnically cleansed to a higher degree by three percentage points than the one under HVO control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but it does not reflect the fact that maybe there was more of an ethnic cleansing there. It does not. 1,200 people were moved from that area and from your area 6,000 people were moved, so I do not know if that data shows you -- judge for yourself. What is more, 6,500 versus 1,200?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Those are absolute numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Had it been for the same methods used, unfortunately they were not the same methods used.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Okay, what I am interested in now is whether you know what methods were used during the ethnic cleansing of Bosniaks, as you call them; that is, did you statistically research how many Bosniaks left for criminal activities, how many exchanged, how many due to direct forcing out of houses? Did you statistically research that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but for God's sake, what kind of crime can you talk about when they could not -- they did not dare open up the doors? If they are in the basement in the Workers' University and if the HVO is taking them out to dig trenches and they do not know if they are coming back --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am sorry, you did not understand me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am sorry, what I meant was not that they engaged in the acts of crime; whether because their houses were looted and there was force used against them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is absurd. If the person may only think how to stay alive, you cannot speak of pillage and rape and things like that. People are trying to stay alive. None of these people whom I interviewed could think in his dream in this way. It has nothing to do with the real situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: My question was whether you tried to identify the actual acts that forced people to leave, the kinds of acts and the people who committed them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is as if I asked you whether you were in Hawaii on vacation. That is what you asked me, more or less. I do not understand this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let us try to keep things calm here, not express too many opinions, too many judgements, and be attentive to the interpreters who are also getting tired. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe we have a misunderstanding here. My question was simply whether you tried to establish in these interviews, or through any statistical method, how many people fled because of certain acts of violence and whether these acts of violence have been identified and enumerated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I identified the acts of violence perpetrated by the HVO against them. I know the forms in which they were forced to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This is the meaning of my question. How many people fled because the military attacked? How many people fled because some member of the HVO or some groups of the HVO broke into the house, pillaged and kicked them out? In that sense, do you have the data?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have all the data.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please go ahead and present it to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 1,500 people from the urban area were expelled by the HVO, by different forms of pressure. Expulsion from the apartments, threats, things like that. From Ahmici, 508 people. On the morning of 16th April, 117 people were killed in Ahmici and 25th May local commune. Some of them were detained in the primary school in Dubravica and some managed to flee to so-called Upper Ahmici and from there to cross over to Vrhovine, which was under BiH army control. The local commune of Gacice, one part of civilians on 20th April 1993 managed to flee across Zabrde to Novi Travnik and the rest of the population was collected by the HVO and brought in front of the department store in Vitez and they told them, "Let the BiH army shoot at you now", and then they were taken in the direction of Travnik and Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: They did not take them back to Gacice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They only took them back for two or three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And today, there are no Bosniaks in Gacice, there are none.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How many people left Gacice in this manner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All 320 of however many live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So some left with the military and others --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, only 30 or 40 managed to flee across the woods. No military there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well, proceed please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I already explained Ahmici and 25th May was the adjoining local commune next to Ahmici. 29 people were killed there on the morning during the attack of the HVO. The rest of the population was either in the camp in Dubravica or later released, together with the people who fled through Gornji Ahmici to Vrhovine. The Dubravica local commune, that is the lower part of it which is near the railroad station, from that local commune the population was collected and through the assistance of UNPROFOR was evacuated. In Stari Vitez local commune, the people were able to defend themselves, about 1,100 of them and they were able to stay there. From the part of Rijeka which is also part of the Vranska local commune, another urban area of the town, they were successively driven out and very few are left now. Then there is the Veceriska local commune; they were expelled during the attack of the HVO on 16th April, and then there is Grbavica, which after it fell was cleansed later. So these are the 4,611 Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. One more question. In your research, have you come across a document or any witness who would state or show that General Blaskic ordered the expulsion of certain people, and I here mean Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I had no insight into such documents which would expressly confirm that this was an order by Mr. Blaskic. I have no such proof.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, we are done. Mr. President, this completes our cross-examination. Mr. Kajmovic, good luck with your thesis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no additional questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, I would appreciate your giving us your unequivocal assessment of some of the issues raised here. You spoke of ethnic cleansing and you mentioned the means which were used in ethnic cleansing. You spoke of breaking into houses as a means of pressure to kick people out, of abuses, different abuse of people, of crossing a frontier under army control, and then you mentioned genocide in Ahmici. Do you consider that genocide was used as one of the means of ethnic cleansing in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my thesis, I touch on the issue of the genocide in Ahmici. I did research this issue and I identified the exact number of victims there, and I tried to ascertain the reasons why this was done and why in Ahmici, and apart from the general motives, there were some local or practical reasons as well. One of the practical reasons for this genocide was that this local commune, where there were 508 Bosniaks, was on the road Vitez-Busovaca. It was a strategically important point and only at this point was there any danger that it could be cut off, and that the HVO may not be able to use it for military purposes. So this was one of the motives, to take control of this road communications, and this would be the purely military aspect of it. But there is another aspect why the genocide was committed there. One was the motivation which was revenge, and on 18th October 1992, when the HVO attacked Novi Travnik, on the orders of the commander Hadzihasanovic of the III Corps, a roadblock or barricade was put up in Ahmici. It was attacked by the HVO and it was removed within about one hour of gunfire, and one young man from Ahmici died, so this barricade briefly slowed down the HVO troops' movement from Busovaca, Kiseljak and Fojnica who were going to Novi Travnik to take control of it and to link up to the forces from Gornji Vakuf. General Blaskic and some other HVO structures said publicly that they would avenge themselves on Ahmici for this barricade, so that when --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who said that? Who said there will be a revenge of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dario Kordic said this on television, that he would avenge himself on the population of Ahmici for the barricades that they put up on 19th October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you see that yourself? Did you see that on television yourself? General Blaskic was with him at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say whether he was there or not, I am not sure, but I am certain of the statement, that it was delivered in the form of a threat. But let me just finish my comment. So there was the aspect of revenge for that barricade which had been put up there, and another reason can be gleaned from the name of that operation, 48 Hours of Ashes. So from a military point of view, it should have been completed within 48 hours, and the effect of such a swift action psychologically speaking, if you do something, such a drastic act, people are brought in a state of shock and indeed all Bosniaks were in a state of shock when they learned of it. So it is the psychological factor, and it was to achieve a certain goal psychologically that should have helped the HVO general goals. So this is what I know and as far as the causes and orders, they probably came from higher levels and probably not from Bosnia-Herzegovina. But this was on a local level, the motivation to commit this genocide precisely in Ahmici and for these specific reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You mentioned that the operation was called 48 Hours of Ashes, the name of the operation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 48 Hours of Ashes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was this the military denomination of this action, or was it just the popular word?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to some information that is perhaps still not sufficiently well grounded, I still do not have reliable data on the name of that operation, but according to some information that I obtained, I learned that this operation was called in that way; namely some of our officers in contact with UNPROFOR members saw in their notebook an indication of this HVO operation as 48 Hours of Ashes. Then there was also a widespread conviction among the people that that was how it was named, and there is another reason which again is not sufficiently well-founded; on the mosque of Ahmic Hazim, because he built this mosque which was destroyed, the HVO fighters wrote graffiti which said, "48 Hours of Ashes Dusko will be working as of the 16th." Of course, photographers took pictures of this, these graffiti and I saw in the media some other photographs as well where probably the HVO administration had had this deleted, so I do not have sufficient evidence to claim that that was indeed the name of the operation. But some knowledge that I have referred to does exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that there was a sudden and massive departure of Bosnian Croats on the eve of the attack, it was I think on 15th and 16th April, and you indicated by that that it was a co-ordinated move and a massive move. Would you conclude from that, or did you conclude from that that this sudden move was due to instructions given for a sudden departure, or could it have been the result of being scared that the Bosnian Croats were so scared that they had to leave the area? What was your assessment? Were they under a threat by the Muslims, in other words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to correct you. I did not say that they went en masse. I am referring to the exact figure of 940-something Croats, so a small percentage of those Croats from certain areas, a smaller proportion of them left their homes that night and crossed over to areas that were under firmer control of the HVO. These were small numbers, but on the first day of the conflict, on the 16th in the morning, there were larger numbers of Croats. When I say "somewhat larger", I am thinking of those 400 out of the 940 who moved from the local commune of Poculica to an area which was more firmly controlled by the HVO, because the HVO applied a simple principle: in areas which it did not control, it publicly, through the media, called on the Croats to cross over into the territory under their control, so if we can consider these 400 Croats to be an exodus en masse, they were living in Poculica and the first morning when the conflict started they withdrew to the area under HVO control, so about 840 Croats as a whole were displaced within the Municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So you do not think that this coincided with the attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are movements by Croats as a consequence of the HVO attack on the Bosniaks and as a consequence of the fact that the HVO did not manage to fully gain control of the whole area, so the HVO did not control the Poculica local commune and that is why the Croats moved out, so, from the Bosniak side, absolutely there was no pressure on the Bosnian Croats for them to vacate a certain territory, with, of course, exceptions -- individual cases which may always occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: My last question is: you mentioned, and I hope I understood you rightly, that in the urban areas of Vitez, people who could not get out were arrested and detained. First I would like to know, these people were civilians or were fighters? Then; by whom were they detained and arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the urban part of Vitez, in the town itself, which was under HVO control -- there were two parts of Vitez, the old part and the new part of the town, the old part most often being referred to as Stari Vitez. In the new part, there were between 1,500 and 1,600 Bosniaks and they could not move out anywhere from there, except through exchanges or through expulsions across the lines. Therefore this part needs to be dealt with separately. In Stari Vitez, there were about 1,100 Bosniaks and there were still some 40 Croats living there and this was a single ethnic population of one ethnicity and this part was also surrounded and they too could not move for eleven and a half months that the war went on, because the HVO had them encircled, but there were combat operations there in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: There were combat, or no combat operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When talking about Stari Vitez --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The last word you mentioned. You said there were no combat operations in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So military people were fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were. No I think we need a map. Can I use the map to explain this? The map of the separation of military forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Dubuisson, that would be in the second package.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Military separation so as to show --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That is what, 192?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, 195, or even 196.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can we use this one? Can I have this one? When mentioning Stari Vitez, I am referring to this part, this area here, which is the area of about 0.3 kilometres, square kilometres, 0.3 square kilometres, and there were about 1,100 inhabitants, mostly Bosniaks, living there. They too, on 16th April in the morning at 4.30, they were attacked by the HVO, but the HVO did not manage to capture it, so that this area was surrounded by HVO territory and HVO front-lines, and this area remained in a situation of combat until 25th February 1994. So there were 1,100 Bosniaks who were still living there. However there are 1,600 of them down here, this part of the town itself. They were not in a classical encirclement of the HVO, but were under the HVO administration. The HVO could arrest, evict and so on, and they actually did. The HVO did not imprison anyone from Stari Vitez; why? Because they could not enter it, but from this other part of the town, these were civilians, there was no army there, and people from 18 onwards were detained and taken to camps, the Workers' University, the SDK, the veterinary station, Dubravica and so on, from this other part of the town which you cannot see on the map, but it is here, the new part of the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So they were civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I do not have any questions as questions themselves, but I have a comment. What disturbs me insofar as your -- let me turn to the Prosecutor. Insofar as your testimony is both the product of scientific research, statistical research and also one that one might call a political testimony, because you have a thesis which corresponds to what you believe and to your commitments in the SDA and -- as a judge, I am somewhat disturbed that you have this thesis which is yours, which is being used by the Prosecution, but at the same time you are presenting your work as a scientific work carried out by an academic at a high level, and you have said this both for the Prosecution and the Defence. I say this to you, because we are entitled to ask for the work to be produced. Of course we are wondering whether this would not disturb you, because you have not yet defended your thesis. We are thinking about a decision which we will not take tonight. I would like to know whether this would disturb you, whether it would cause any problems for you, that is to give us the work in the state that it is right now. As I say, my concern is that it is a scientific work, but you are not absolutely an expert such as the Prosecution witnesses that have been called in, university professors who are not involved in the conflict. You have a thesis, it is your right, it is not a criticism that I am making. My question is -- we will not take a decision this evening. The judges will discuss it, but would that be a problem for you in respect of your university, in respect of the completion of your work, would it be problematic for you for that work to be given to the Tribunal as it stands now, and that is both to the Defence and the Prosecution, the Defence that might want to call you back or might want to file an additional brief or an additional reply. You see, that is the basis for my concern. It is not as much the statistics, but rather statistics that are being used to support a thesis. This is the concern that I have, and we would like to have your comments about this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are no problems in that regard. It is possible to communicate this paper, there is no dispute over that, but you must know that from the standpoint of science, a problem has to be studied using sources, and a certain allegation has to be based in certain sources. Therefore to absolutely exclude any political considerations is impossible, because it is not a Master's thesis at a political science faculty and not at the mathematics department. So one may have the impression that politics is playing a part, but in defending certain positions in the paper, I have to refer to certain sources, but certainly not to political convictions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What concerns me -- you see I did hear your answer, but what concerns me are the rights of the Defence and the respect for an inter parte proceeding. Not only was this information not given to the Defence in the proper time, but your explanations were long, I did not interrupt you -- the cross-examination was not always limited to the examination-in-chief, but I did not interrupt, because I think for the Defence the situation was a bit difficult, because in the end it -- your answers were both political and statistical. Therefore if you were being asked political questions, you could answer with mathematics and if you were being asked about statistics for which it did not have effects, you defended yourself with your convictions. That is your political thesis. I have simply noted down: we will not take a decision tonight, the judges will reflect about it, but I have noted that partially or fully, you would not find yourself in any difficulties vis-à-vis your university to give the information to the Tribunal, which is entitled to in fact demand it. This would help the future of the proceedings as we go forward. Do you have any comments you would like to make about this, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I would like at the end to draw attention to a legal practice, a norm as it is regulated in the country I come from. Actually in the legal system that I am working in, the expert witness is always and exclusively an independent person. His exemption may be required if he has personal links with the subject in dispute. I know that the Statute of the Tribunal has not regulated these matters fully, but I think that one might make an objection and say that this witness is most directly involved with the case in dispute, because he was at the head of the party that formed the army in Vitez that was opposed to the HVO. He was one of the leaders of the people fighting the HVO, and this disqualifies him as an objective expert witness. So will you please bear this in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we did not conceal that fact when we offered Mr. Kajmovic to your Honours and his statistical report and analysis. That issue, of whether Mr. Kajmovic had an active part in the civic and political affairs of his community was brought out on direct examination. There was no effort to conceal that. I would submit, Mr. President, there are not a lot of people who have conducted a study on the demographic changes in the Vitez Municipality, given the tremendously difficult circumstances, one can imagine conducting such a study would entail. We have endeavoured to bring to your Honours' attention a report from a source who was formerly the President of the SDA, but your Honours can judge his credibility in assessing his testimony and the accuracy of the statistical data he has presented to you, particularly in light of the previous testimony that your Honours have heard about what happened in the villages about which he has testified and provided you with statistical data. For example, you have heard, Mr. President, from independent sources, from sources such as UNPROFOR and ECMM, that there are no people left, no Muslims left, in the village of Ahmici. That is something that has been corroborated by these statistics. I would ask you, Mr. President, when you bear in mind the source of this report, Mr. Kajmovic and his past political interests, that you also bear in mind the other testimonies that you have heard in this case in respect of what happened in various villages, what happened in terms of the meanings and methods that have been described by this witness through the testimonies of other witnesses. That is all I am saying, Mr. President. I do not think that I take issue with Mr. Nobilo's comment to disqualify Mr. Kajmovic. I would submit that Mr. Kajmovic is a witness who bears listening to and it is up to your Honours as professional judges to weigh his interest and his information that he has provided to you in the context of this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I would put things back into proper proportions. I must say that there was no lack of fairness on the part of the Prosecutor, because he stated in the beginning of the testimony, during the summary before the witness came in, that the witness had a significant political commitment with the Muslim community. There were no problems on that. If in absolute terms Mr. Nobilo's comment is valid, for today, nothing is amiss. But my second comment, which is something which I have already said several times, the judges must evaluate, given the context in all of these situations the true reliability, as they say in my system, the probative value or the weight of this or that testimony. That is the work of the judges and they will do that work, but the question that is for the judges to be able to do their work, I would like to know whether this cross-examination was able to take place under the best conditions, and I would like certainly to point out a few things. Now that we have heard what you have to say, the decision will be taken. I think we do not need to have the next witness brought in. The day has been long, but from now on this Trial Chamber intends, and I say this for the interpreters, to begin at 2.00, except for some days, when there may be lunches that take longer or invitations that arrive, but ordinarily, this chamber will start to sit at 2.00 and will stop at 6.30, with an attempt at a 20-minute break in the middle. We will try to stick to that schedule which will be better for the judges and I hope it will not be too disturbing for the work of the interpreters. Thank you very much, we will resume tomorrow at 2.00. (6.55 pm)
